summary: ModGovernor is a 229-line Governor-Bravo-shaped contract: anyone above proposalThreshold proposes a batch of (target, value, calldata), holders vote with `votes.balanceOf(msg.sender)` read at the moment they vote, and once the period ends anyone can execute a proposal whose forVotes exceed againstVotes and a quorum of `votes.totalSupply() * quorumBps / 10000`; it outputs the `governor` port, which the canvas installs as the `owner` of every block wired to it, so a passed proposal is an arbitrary call from the address that owns the whole deployment. The worst finding is the vote-weight read itself: because weight is the live balance and the `votes` input is a plain `erc20` port, any transferable token (the catalog's own ModToken included) lets one wallet vote, transfer to a fresh wallet, and vote again without limit, so one token unit and a few transfers out-vote the whole supply and hand the attacker setOwner() on every wired block. Even with the recommended vote-escrow, `state()` is recomputed live with no snapshot and no execution expiry, so a proposal that lost on quorum silently becomes executable when the escrow supply decays; the timelock is optional per-call (execute() on an un-queued Succeeded proposal calls targets directly, and the queued path actually reverts NOT_OWNER for governor-owned blocks); and the guardian, which defaults to the deployer's EOA, can point `timelock` at itself and rewrite quorum/period/threshold single-handedly. Not safe to deploy as-is with a transferable vote token; with a vote-escrow token and a guardian the community trusts it is a 1-hour-race-to-capture contract, not a governance contract.

findings.title: Vote weight is the live balanceOf at vote time: with any transferable vote token one wallet's tokens vote unlimited times (transfer-and-revote, or flash-loan), capturing every block the governor owns
findings.where: castVote() L148-L158 (weight = votes.balanceOf(msg.sender) L151, hasVoted keyed per address L150/L153); catalog input `votes` type `erc20`; ERC20Base has no checkpoints (common.sol L54-L118)
findings.detail: castVote reads `votes.balanceOf(msg.sender)` at the moment of the call and dedupes only by (proposal, address). Nothing snapshots balances at proposal start and ERC20Base carries no checkpointing, so the same tokens can be moved to a new address and voted again for as long as the proposal is Active (a minimum of one hour, three days by default). The header comment and catalog docs admit this and say the 'natural' token is the vote-escrow, but the `votes` port is typed `erc20`, so the composer happily wires ModToken (or any external ERC20) and nothing in the constructor rejects a transferable token. Because the canvas passes `$input:governor` as the `owner` of every wired block (token, vault, lending, oracle, cdp, psm, treasury, etc.), one passed proposal is a batch of onlyOwner calls from the address that owns the whole protocol: setOwner(attacker) everywhere, mint() on the token, setPrice() on the oracle, sweep on the treasury. Quorum is no defence: it is a percentage of totalSupply and the attacker's effective weight is unbounded (N transfers = N x balance).
findings.exploit: 1. Deployment wires ModToken (transferable, 1,000,000 supply) into governor.votes, quorumBps 400, and the governor as owner of a vault, an oracle and the token. 2. Attacker buys or borrows 1,000 tokens (0.1% of supply). 3. Attacker calls propose([token, vault, oracle], [0,0,0], [setOwner(attacker) x3], 'maintenance'). 4. After votingDelay, from wallet A: castVote(id, true) -> +1,000. transfer(B, 1000); from B castVote(id, true) -> +1,000. Repeat 50 times across the voting period (or in one tx via a helper contract that loops fresh CREATE2 addresses): forVotes = 50,000 >= quorum 40,000, from only 1,000 real tokens. A flash loan of the token makes the same thing free in one block. 5. After p.end anyone calls execute(id): three direct calls from the governor succeed, attacker owns the token (mints unlimited), the vault (setStrategy / fees), and the oracle (setPrice -> drains lending/cdp). Total loss of every asset in every governor-owned block.
findings.recommendation: Snapshot voting power: require the vote token to expose getPastVotes(account, blockNumber)/getPastTotalSupply (ERC20Votes) and record `snapshot = block.number` (or timestamp) in propose(), reading weight and quorum from that snapshot in castVote()/state(). If the block must stay ERC20-shaped, change the `votes` input to the `escrow` port type only and have the constructor verify non-transferability (e.g. staticcall transfer() and require revert, or require a `locks()`/`maxLock()` selector). At minimum reject transferable tokens in the catalog UI and refuse to wire ModToken into `votes`.

findings.title: Outcome is recomputed live against a moving totalSupply and never expires: a proposal that lost on quorum becomes executable later as escrow weight decays or tokens burn, and a passed one can be flipped to Defeated by minting
findings.where: state() L110-L119 (quorum() re-read on every call L116); quorum() L106-L108; execute() L173-L188 (no deadline / grace period)
findings.detail: state() has no stored result: after p.end it re-evaluates `p.forVotes < quorum()` against `votes.totalSupply()` at the moment of the call, while forVotes/againstVotes are frozen sums recorded at vote time. There is no grace period, so a Succeeded proposal is executable forever. With the recommended ModVoteEscrow, totalSupply() decays linearly to zero as locks expire (veescrow.sol L65-L82), so quorum() only ever falls between relock events; with ModToken, public burn() (token.sol L31-L33) lowers supply and owner mint() raises it. The result is a non-monotonic state machine: (a) a hostile batch that was Defeated on quorum flips to Succeeded, with no new vote, once supply has decayed or been burned below forVotes/quorumBps, and anyone may execute it at that moment; (b) whoever controls token supply (the token owner, or the governor itself via an earlier proposal) can push a legitimately passed-but-not-yet-executed proposal back to Defeated by minting, or un-brick a Queued one by burning. Because proposalThreshold starts at 0 (GOVERNOR-4) planting such sleeper proposals is free.
findings.exploit: 1. Governor.votes = ModVoteEscrow; active locked weight 1,000,000 (quorum 4% = 40,000). 2. Attacker locks a modest amount and proposes [treasury.setOwner(attacker), token.setOwner(attacker)] with a bland description, votes for with 5,000 weight; nobody votes against (it is one of many spam proposals). After p.end state() = Defeated (5,000 < 40,000) and everyone forgets it. 3. Twelve months later most locks have expired or been withdrawn and nobody relocked: totalSupply() = 90,000, quorum() = 3,600. state(id) now returns Succeeded. 4. Attacker calls execute(id): the year-old proposal runs, taking ownership of the treasury and the token. No vote happened in the interval and the description is stale. Griefing variant: a ModToken-owned-by-EOA governor; the community passes 'raise the vault fee cap', and before anyone executes, the token owner mints 50% more supply so quorum() jumps above forVotes and the proposal is Defeated.
findings.recommendation: Snapshot quorum: store `quorumVotes = quorum()` (or the totalSupply) in the Proposal at propose()/at the start of voting and compare against that. Store the terminal outcome once (e.g. a `finalize()` or lazily on the first post-end call) so it cannot move. Add an execution deadline (Bravo's GRACE_PERIOD, e.g. 14 days after end/eta) after which the state is Expired and execute() reverts.

findings.title: Timelock is bypassable per proposal and does not actually work for governor-owned blocks: execute() on an un-queued Succeeded proposal calls targets directly, while the queued path reverts NOT_OWNER
findings.where: execute() L173-L188 (branch on `p.eta != 0` L180, direct call L183); queue() L162-L171; state() L117-L118; catalog wire timelock.setAdmin(governor); every block ctor `$input:governor|$owner`
findings.detail: queue() is optional. execute() accepts state Succeeded (never queued, eta == 0) as well as Queued, and in the Succeeded case it performs `p.targets[i].call(...)` from the governor itself, regardless of whether a timelock is wired. So the 'delay' the catalog promises ('wire a timelock and ... passed proposals execute through the delay') is a courtesy the executor may decline: anyone can call execute(id) the second the vote closes. Worse, the queued path is broken for the wiring the catalog produces. The canvas sets each block's owner to the address of whichever `governor`-typed block is connected. If that is the ModGovernor, then a queued proposal executes via ModTimelock.execute(), whose `target.call` has msg.sender = timelock, and every Owned block reverts NOT_OWNER -> CALL_FAILED, and since p.eta is now non-zero the direct path is closed too: the proposal is permanently stuck in Queued. If instead blocks are owned by the timelock, the direct path is what reverts and the delay is enforced, but nothing tells the deployer which wiring they are in. Either way the timelock cannot be relied on, and the one configuration where it works is the one the governor's docs do not describe.
findings.exploit: 1. Deploy token + vault + governor + timelock(48h); wire timelock into governor.timelock (composer calls timelock.setAdmin(governor)); wire governor into vault.governor so vault.owner = governor. 2. A proposal 'vault.setOwner(attacker)' passes (see GOVERNOR-1 for how cheap that is). 3. Watchers expect 48h to unwind positions. Instead, in the same block p.end passes, attacker calls governor.execute(id) without ever calling queue(): state == Succeeded, eta == 0, branch at L182 executes `vault.call(setOwner(attacker))` directly from the governor -> succeeds instantly. 4. Conversely, an honest executor who calls queue(id) first gets eta set; 48h later execute(id) routes through timelock.execute -> vault.setOwner from msg.sender = timelock -> 'NOT_OWNER' -> CALL_FAILED; the honest proposal is bricked and must be re-proposed and executed the fast way.
findings.recommendation: When a timelock is set, make queueing mandatory: in execute() require `address(timelock) == address(0) || p.eta != 0`, and in queue() require state Succeeded (already done). Decide one ownership model and enforce it: either (a) the governor is a thin voting layer and the TIMELOCK owns the blocks (Bravo model) — then remove the direct-call branch entirely and have the composer wire `$input:governor` to the timelock address when the governor has one; or (b) the governor owns the blocks and the timelock is an internal delay — then have the timelock call back into the governor (an `executeQueued(id)` entrypoint restricted to the timelock) so the outbound call comes from the governor. Document which one in the catalog `docs`.

findings.title: Guardian (the deployer's EOA by default) can rewrite quorum, period, delay and threshold single-handedly by pointing `timelock` at itself, and can drop the timelock at will — it 'can never pass one' is false
findings.where: setTimelock() L218-L221 (guardian may set any address, including an EOA or address(0)); setParams() L203-L216 (accepts msg.sender == address(timelock) L209); cancel() L191-L197 (guardian veto on any proposal); constructor L73 (guardian = $owner)
findings.detail: setParams is meant to be governance-only, but it also trusts `address(timelock)`, and setTimelock lets the guardian install any address there with no vote and no delay. The guardian therefore has a two-call path to `setParams(0, 1 hours, 0, 0)`: zero voting delay, one-hour period (the constructor minimum), zero threshold, zero quorum. Combined with the guardian's unconditional cancel() over every other proposal, a competing community cannot use governance to respond. The guardian can also call setTimelock(0) at any moment, removing whatever delay a wired timelock provided, and setGuardian() is guardian-only so the community can never remove a rogue guardian by vote (setGuardian is not callable by address(this) or the timelock). The catalog passes `$owner` — the deploying wallet — as guardian, so in practice one hot key holds a 1-hour-race-to-capture over every governor-owned block, and the header comment 'The guardian can stop a proposal but can never pass one' is untrue.
findings.exploit: 1. Guardian G (deployer EOA) holds 1 wei of the vote token (or a tiny escrow lock). 2. G calls setTimelock(G). 3. G calls setParams(0, 3600, 0, 0) — passes the GOVERNANCE_ONLY check because msg.sender == timelock. 4. G calls setTimelock(address(0)) so execute() takes the direct path. 5. At 03:00 UTC G proposes [every block].setOwner(G) + token.mint(G, 1e30); voting opens immediately (delay 0). 6. G casts 1 wei for. Any counter-proposal the community raises is cancel()ed by G. If holders do not out-vote 1 wei within 60 minutes, at minute 61 G calls execute(id): quorum is 0, forVotes 1 > againstVotes 0, and G owns the protocol. Lesser variant with no vote at all: G calls setTimelock(0) minutes before a hostile proposal's execution to strip the 48h exit window users were counting on.
findings.recommendation: Restrict setTimelock to `msg.sender == address(this)` (a passed proposal), or at least require the new address to have code and respond to delay(). Drop `msg.sender == address(timelock)` from setParams unless GOVERNOR-3(b) is adopted, in which case route it through a dedicated timelock-only entrypoint. Make setGuardian callable by governance (address(this)/timelock) so a rogue guardian can be removed, and consider making guardian cancel() valid only while a proposal is Pending/Active/Queued (not after Succeeded) or time-boxing the guardian role. Never leave the guardian as a single hot EOA in a real deployment.

findings.title: proposalThreshold is hard-wired to 0 at deploy and not a catalog param: anyone can create unlimited proposals, and only a passed proposal can raise it
findings.where: propose() L121-L146 (require balanceOf >= proposalThreshold L129, threshold is 0 until setParams); state variable L29; catalog `params` (no threshold); setParams() L203-L216
findings.detail: The constructor does not take a proposal threshold and the catalog exposes none, so the deployed value is 0 and `votes.balanceOf(msg.sender) >= 0` is true for every address, including ones with no tokens. Any EOA can push arbitrary-length batches into `proposals` (each with a stored description string and calldata), flooding proposalCount()/the console with hostile lookalike proposals. Each is a live trap under GOVERNOR-2 (sleeper proposals that later meet a decayed quorum) and under GOVERNOR-1 (any one of them can be passed by transfer-voting). Raising the threshold requires a proposal that itself has to pass, and setParams caps nothing, so a passed proposal can also set threshold above totalSupply or votingDelay to centuries and brick proposing permanently (recoverable only by the guardian's escalation in GOVERNOR-4).
findings.exploit: 1. Governor deployed from the catalog with default params; proposalThreshold == 0. 2. A wallet holding zero vote tokens calls propose([vault], [0], [setOwner(attacker)], 'Bump performance fee to 8%') 500 times in a loop over a few days, each with a different plausible description. 3. Token holders cannot tell hostile from honest batches without decoding calldata for each; against-votes are spread thin; a single one that nobody votes against sits Defeated on quorum and is executable later per GOVERNOR-2, or is pushed through by transfer-voting per GOVERNOR-1.
findings.recommendation: Add `proposalThreshold_` to the constructor and the catalog params with a non-zero default (e.g. 0.5–1% of initial supply, expressed in token units or bps of totalSupply), require a snapshot balance in propose(), and bound setParams (votingDelay <= 2 weeks, votingPeriod <= 4 weeks, threshold <= 10% of supply). Bravo also lets anyone cancel a proposal whose proposer has dropped below threshold — add that so proposers cannot borrow their way past the gate.

findings.title: Composition: the vote token's minter controls the governor — a mintable ModToken owned by an EOA lets that key mint a majority, and a token owned by the governor lets one passed proposal mint a permanent majority
findings.where: castVote() L151 and quorum() L107 (both read the live token); token.sol mint() L26-L29 (onlyOwner, unbounded); catalog token ctor `$input:governor|$owner`
findings.detail: Voting power and quorum are whatever `votes` reports. ModToken.mint() is unbounded and onlyOwner, and the catalog defaults `mintable_` on with the owner being either the deployer's wallet or, if wired, the governor. If the token owner is an EOA, that key can at any time mint itself 51%+ of supply (or more than quorum + current forVotes), vote, and take ownership of every governor-owned block — governance reduces to the token-owner's key, which is invisible to the other blocks that believe they are 'governed'. If the token owner is the governor, any proposal that passes once (see GOVERNOR-1/4 for how cheaply) can include `token.mint(attacker, hugeAmount)` and thereby lock in control of every future vote, because there is no cap, no snapshot and no minting delay. With the vote-escrow, the same applies one hop up: minting the underlying token and locking it for maxLock yields dominant escrow weight in one block.
findings.exploit: 1. Canvas: ModToken(mintable, owner = deployer EOA D) -> governor.votes; governor owns vault, cdp, oracle. Users believe those blocks are controlled by token holders. 2. D calls token.mint(D, 10 x totalSupply), proposes oracle.setPrice(0.01) + cdp.setOwner(D), votes for with 91% of supply, executes after the period, and liquidates every cdp position at a false price. Variant: token.owner = governor; attacker passes one proposal (GOVERNOR-1) whose first action is token.mint(attacker, 1e30); every subsequent proposal is decided by the attacker alone, forever.
findings.recommendation: Deploy the vote token with mintable_ = false, or mint through a separate minter with a hard cap and a timelock; if the governor must own a mintable token, gate mint() behind the timelock and put a per-epoch cap in the token. Document in the catalog that `votes` must be a fixed-supply or escrow token and that whoever can mint it owns the governor.

findings.title: Without a timelock wired (the default), passed proposals execute the moment voting closes, so users of governed blocks get no exit window
findings.where: execute() L173-L188 (direct call branch L182-L185); catalog timelock input `required: false`, ctor `$input:timelock|$zero`
findings.detail: The timelock input is optional and defaults to $zero. With no timelock, the only delay between a hostile proposal being submitted and its execution is votingDelay + votingPeriod (1h + 3d by default, and the guardian can push that to 0 + 1h per GOVERNOR-4). Depositors in a vault, cdp or lending block owned by the governor have to watch the proposal list and act before p.end, because anyone can call execute() in the very block after p.end. This is intended by the block's design ('without it a proposal executes directly') but it is the setting every template will land on, and it compounds every other finding here.
findings.exploit: 1. Governor deployed with no timelock; owns lending (oracle owner) and vault. 2. Hostile proposal passes at timestamp T = p.end (via GOVERNOR-1, or an honest majority that a minority disagrees with). 3. At T+1 the proposer calls execute(id) -> oracle.setPrice(...)/vault.setOwner(...); users who intended to withdraw after the result was known find the change already in force in the same block they learned the outcome.
findings.recommendation: Make the timelock input required (or default the composer to dropping a ModTimelock on the canvas whenever a governor is added) and fix GOVERNOR-3 so the delay is actually enforced. Alternatively enforce a built-in minimum `executionDelay` in the governor between p.end and execute().

findings.title: cancel() does not clear timelock entries, proposers can cancel after passing, and a batch with two identical actions can never be queued
findings.where: cancel() L191-L197; queue() L162-L171 (salt = bytes32(id) L167); timelock.sol queue() L35-L41 (`require(queuedAt[id] == 0)`)
findings.detail: Three small correctness gaps around the queue: (1) cancel() on a Queued proposal flips p.cancelled but leaves each action's queuedAt entry in ModTimelock; nothing in the governor ever calls timelock.cancel(), so stale executable operations accumulate under the governor's admin key and would become live if the timelock's admin is ever moved to another controller by a proposal. (2) The proposer keeps a unilateral cancel() right at any stage up to execution (Bravo only allows this while the proposer is below threshold), so a proposer can let a proposal pass, watch users reposition, and cancel at the last moment — cheap griefing, also usable to withdraw a decoy while a sleeper (GOVERNOR-2) stays. (3) Two actions with identical (target, value, calldata) in one batch hash to the same timelock id because the salt is per-proposal, so timelock.queue reverts QUEUED on the second and the proposal cannot be queued — it can only be executed via the direct path, silently skipping the delay.
findings.exploit: 1. Proposal id 7 with actions [vault.setFee(100), vault.setFee(100)] passes. queue(7) reverts 'QUEUED' on the second action. execute(7) with eta == 0 runs both directly, no delay. 2. Proposal id 8 (treasury.setOwner(X)) is queued, then cancel(8) by the proposer: governor state is Cancelled but ModTimelock.queuedAt[hash(treasury, 0, setOwner(X), 8)] remains set, and if a later proposal calls timelock.setAdmin(newController), newController can execute that stale operation.
findings.recommendation: In cancel(), if p.eta != 0 loop the actions and call timelock.cancel(timelock.hash(target, value, data, bytes32(id))). Use a per-action salt (keccak256(id, i)) so duplicate actions queue. Restrict proposer cancel to Pending/Active, or to the case where the proposer's balance has fallen below proposalThreshold (and let anyone cancel in that case).

safe_use: Only wire a non-transferable vote weight into `votes`: a ModVoteEscrow lock (or an external ERC20Votes-style token with checkpoints). Never wire ModToken or any transferable ERC20 — one holder can vote the same tokens as many times as they have addresses.

Do not make the vote token (or the escrow's underlying token) mintable, or if it must be, keep mint() behind a capped, timelocked minter. Whoever can mint votes owns the governor and everything it owns.

Treat the guardian as a full admin key, not a veto: it can drop the timelock and rewrite quorum/period/threshold via setTimelock(self) -> setParams. Use a multisig, or set guardian to a burn address once the deployment is stable (there is no governance path to replace a rogue guardian).

If you want a real delay, own the blocks with the ModTimelock, not the ModGovernor, and understand that until execute() requires queueing, anyone can still execute an un-queued Succeeded proposal directly from the governor — the direct path must be removed for the timelock to bind.

Set a non-zero proposalThreshold with the first proposal after deploy (it is 0 at construction and not a catalog param), and cap votingDelay/votingPeriod there too; the constructor bounds nothing but period >= 1h and quorum <= 100%.

Because outcomes are recomputed live and never expire, periodically cancel (as guardian) every Defeated proposal so it cannot flip to Succeeded as escrow weight decays, and execute or cancel Succeeded proposals promptly.

Watch proposals, not just execution: with no timelock the change lands in the block after the vote closes. Depositors in governor-owned vaults/cdps/lending should exit before p.end of any proposal they distrust.
